utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case Number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow what I'm saying in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Ms. Korner, appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman with David Cunningham, and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you and good afternoon to you. Any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one, Your Honour, and that's this. Although I spoke to Mr. Ackerman, but I would just like it confirmed on the record, that the question of whether there would be witnesses from Glamoc, Laktasi, and Srbac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham told us to expect a reply today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good or bad news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already told Ms. Korner there would be no witnesses from those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So before we bring in the witness, there are no protective measures, Mr. Ackerman? And we are all agreed that I should give him a caution before he starts testifying?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, he's Mr. Ackerman's witness, so I think perhaps Mr. Ackerman should go first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no such request. If Your Honour feels you should do that, go ahead. But I have not requested it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, good afternoon to you, Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are about to start giving evidence as a witness produced by the accused Radoslav Brdjanin in this trial. And our rules require that before you do so, you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam usher is going to hand you the text of this solemn declaration. That is equivalent to an oath. And I would now invite you to read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is not the first time you're giving evidence in a court, no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have testified before the OTP. I have never testified before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I'll explain to you very briefly what the procedure is because giving a statement during an interview is one thing. Testifying in open court is another. What's going to happen is that Mr. Ackerman, who is the lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin - correct me if I am wrong, Mr. Ackerman - will be leading the examination-in-chief. He will be putting to you a series of questions to which you need to answer. He will then be followed by Ms. Korner, who is the lead counsel for the Prosecution, in a series -- with a series of questions. And that exercise we usually refer to as cross-examination. Although you are a witness summoned by the accused himself, it doesn't mean to say that you have come here to testify what is in favour of the accused and not what is or could be against him. In fact, you are under an obligation here to answer all questions irrespective of who is putting the question to you, be it Mr. Ackerman or Ms. Korner, in line with the oath that you've taken a couple of minutes ago. Your obligation under the law is to answer each question truthfully and as fully as possible. You are also one of the protagonists in the events that took place in 1992, which is the period that we are dealing with. And it is my duty to caution you that if there are any questions put to you by whoever, that if you answer could expose you to criminal proceedings before this Tribunal or elsewhere, then you have a right to ask me as the Presiding Judge to be exempted from answering that particular question. You do not have an automatic right. That's something that Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and Judge Taya from Japan will discuss as and if the question arises. And then we will let you know what our decision is. Otherwise, your obligation is to answer every question that is put to you, although there may be instances when we ourselves will tell you, "Mr. Radic, you don't need to answer this question." Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ackerman, he is all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had -- just so you know, I had prepared this examination to use the new technology provided by the Sanction programme fully expecting that the technology people would have installed the VGA cord that I needed here since I requested it almost a week ago. It's not here. It's apparently more of a challenge than they're up to. So hopefully within the next month or so, they'll get that done and we can actually start using the same technology that the Prosecutor uses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that you are not asking for an adjournment of a month, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, okay, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it would be a waste of time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, your name is Predrag Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Radic, you were president of the Banja Luka Assembly or, as some people call you, the mayor of Banja Luka during the year 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. When you say that I was a mayor, I wasn't. I was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand that many people have referred to you as the mayor of Banja Luka, though, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to first tell the Judges about your educational background, degrees you might have earned, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Shall I start with the beginning then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th of January 1941 in Gradiska. I completed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. my elementary education there, and two lower grades of the grammar school. I completed my grammar school education in Banja Luka. I graduated from the school of economics in Belgrade. Then I completed my post-graduate studies at the school of engineering in Belgrade. I defended my doctoral thesis at the school of economics in Banja Luka, and this is where I hold a tenure, and I teach the planning in production.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you an engineer or an economist or what are you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I'm an economist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you elected president of the Banja Luka Municipality? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: At the democratic elections in 1990, I was elected president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. At that time, it was not a town yet. It was just a municipality. And nowadays, Banja Luka is a town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what party were you a member of during those elections?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of any party. What I was asked to do is to give my consent to be put forward by the Serbian Democratic Party. But I wasn't a member of any party. I was just on the list of the Serbian Democratic Party at the moment of these elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the Serbian Democrat Party?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: After the elections, because it didn't make much sense for me to be a candidate without actually being a member of the party after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you still a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not. After the Dayton Accords, I was the presiding person of the coalition of the Democratic Patriotic Bloc. After the elections, I was removed from the SDS list. I was discharged of my duties of the president of the assembly of the town of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you belong to any political party at the present time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was the one who actually established the democratic patriotic party, and I'm its president. It is a small party, but it does have seats in the parliament. It does have its representatives in the city assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And today you're the head of that party. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you back now to 1992 and ask you if you recall early April of 1992. I think perhaps the 3rd of April of 1992 when a group called SOS set up barricades in Banja Luka. Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall that they -- one of the requests that they made was that a crisis staff be set up?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I remember that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen? Was a crisis staff set up at their request?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The crisis staff was set up, and from the documents that I had the opportunity to see I know who the members of the crisis staff were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court - and while you're telling the Court, I'm going to ask that you be given an exhibit. It's -- I believe the exhibit is P137. And it might help you refresh your memory with regard to some of these matters. While that's coming, tell the Court who were the members of that crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I could give you the names of some of them. However, I must tell you that these people were not elected. It was by virtue of their positions that they became members of the crisis staff. So you are going to find the judge of the district court there and another judge who is nowadays a member of the constitutional court of Republika Srpska. You will find the members of some MPs there. The representative of the army of Republika Srpska will also be on that list. You will also find the names of certain people from the police. I was also there in my capacity as the president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. So those names were on the list, and you will find those names in the exhibits that you have at your disposal. I could give you some names. For example, Jovan Rosic, Milan Puvacic, Predrag Radic, Stojan Zupljanin, Colonel and later on General Kelecevic is also mentioned as one of the members and so on and so forth. You have that list. I myself can't remember all of those names after so much time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think maybe we've gotten off the track here. I think you're talking about the ARK Crisis Staff. Are you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the crisis staff formed --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please show me the list. I'm sure you have it. The list must exist because it was published in Glas newspapers, and I'm sure you have taken that document from that paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think P137, and it's there to be handed to you right now.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can actually read it, although it is cut in half. Here you have on behalf of the Banja Luka Municipality Predrag Mitrakovic, who was at that time the secretary of urban planning. There is my name on behalf of the public security centre. Stojan Zupljanin. Then Vladimir Tutus, the head of SJB, the public security service. On behalf of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff, there was Milorad Sajic, Milos Cesic, and Miroslav Vesic. On behalf of the judiciary, members of the crisis staff were Milan Puvacic, Jovo Rosic. The Banja Luka corps was represented --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slow down because we have interpreters having -- slow down please because the interpreters that have to translate translating into English and then to French have to catch up with you. Sometimes it's not easy when you speak so rapidly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the judiciary, Milan Puvacic, Jovo Rosic. On behalf of the Banja Luka corps, Colonel Bosko Koljevic, Bogdan Subotic. On behalf of the political parties, Dr. Radoslav Vukic and Nenad Stevandic. On behalf of the assembly of the ARK Krajina, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin who was a member of the crisis staff. And obviously, those who demanded for the crisis staff to be set up, members of the SOS, on their behalf, or rather they were represented by Ilija Milinkovic, Slobodan Popovic, Aleksandar Tolimir, and Ranko Dubocanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to direct your attention now to a section of that newspaper you have in front of you that's headed "Serbian Defence Forces Proclamation." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me, please. This text that I have in front of me, there are parts missing. It is not complete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see a section that begin -- the headline is "Serbian Defence Forces Proclamation"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. But if you will allow me, I have this document on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you can use your own document or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Apparently the exhibit is incomplete, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is precisely the point. If he's saying that the exhibit is incomplete, I'd like to see where it is incomplete.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not incomplete, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's probably selected. No, and it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he has only been given a part of the exhibit. The exhibit runs to one, two, three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But he's only got one small part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, usher, give the witness my copy. And perhaps he can look at it and tell me if that is complete or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a complete text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Witness, Mr. Radic, could you please go to the part which says "Serbian Defence Forces Proclamation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here it is. That is the bottom part of this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go down a ways in there, you're going to find that after making a statement, then it says this: "Therefore, the statement says `we demand that the president of the municipality activate a crisis staff that we would agree to and negotiate with so as to fulfill the following demands'." And then what you see there is a list of demands. And what I'd like to go is go through those basically one at a time with you and ask you about each one. If you look at the first of those, what is being requested is the immediate enactment of a law on internal affairs of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, would this crisis staff that was put together have had any competence to adopt and enact a law on internal affairs of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The demand is for something else within this proclamation, and you will find that towards the end of this proclamation. They ask for their representative in the assembly of the town of Banja Luka and in the assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. What they demanded was for these decisions to be made by the municipalities and the AR Krajina. They themselves and the municipalities, or even the assembly of AR Krajina could not adopt this law. Although the demand was not for us to adopt the law, but to implement it. In other words, that law allegedly had already been in place, and it only had to be implemented. I don't remember what this law was all about, however we could not implement this law if it hadn't been previously adopted by the National Assembly of Republika Srpska. This would have been beyond the competencies of both the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka as well as of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your interpretation at least of that demand is that they weren't asking this crisis staff to enact a law on internal affairs for the entire republic, but that they were asking that the law on internal affairs be implemented in Banja Luka and the Krajina. Is that your interpretation of that demand?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: How can something be implemented in the town of Banja Luka which is part of Republika Srpska if it isn't implemented in the other parts of Republika Srpska? It was, therefore, impossible to carry this out because further on in the text, it says that it has to be implemented, that a law on internal affairs of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina has to be implemented, and certain markings have to be changed immediately. So the assembly of the town of Banja Luka couldn't have adopted this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second thing --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I assist Mr. Ackerman. I think it's clearer from the actual text of the proclamation than from the Glas article, if one looks at Exhibit P134. It actually uses the word "implemented" as opposed to the word here, which is "enactment."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the second demand now. The second demand is for the immediate change of signs. Do you have any idea what that's all about? Do you know what that demand was, what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I can only guess what this means, since it doesn't state what signs are concerned. And a lot of time has passed. I think that they wanted signs -- institutions of Republika Srpska to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... In the actual text, it's insignia, not "signs." If you go to P134, that's put in front of him, I think you'll see it, rather than going --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that makes sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have P134 made available to the witness as well. Perhaps you could put the English version on the ELMO because we were not prepared for this document. Further down, Madam usher, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir, you'll see there in paragraph 1 that it says that "insignia" be changed immediately. Does that make more sense to you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. To immediately change the insignia, that's what it states in this text here and in the other text that I have in front of me, and I assume that this was insignia in institutes. They wanted insignia in institutes to be changed. And for example, if it was the district court or the Security Services Centre, these belonged to the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They wanted these insignia to be changed, and they wanted the Latin script to be replaced by the Cyrillic script. This is probably what they were requesting because this had already been implemented in Croatia and in the areas where the Bosniaks were in the majority. They had replaced all signs in the Cyrillic script with the Latin script. I think that is what it is about. I don't have any other interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They ask for it to be done immediately. Was it done immediately or was it ever done?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It wasn't done immediately because this didn't fall within the competence of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. And I don't believe that the ARK Assembly could have done this either. This was perhaps a decision perhaps of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, but this happened a lot later and it took a long time for all the names of the towns to be changed. It took a lot of time for the signs for the town of Banja Luka and Zvornik to be changed and to replace them with signs in the Cyrillic script. And perhaps there was a directive that was issued in order to do this from the assembly of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next demand. "That all employees who have shown through their work that they are destroyers of Yugoslavia and enemies of the Serbian People be fired." What was done with that demand?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I have to say that prior to this request, there was an event -- there was something that provoked this entire programme. And that was the referendum that was held in order to have -- obtain the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia. And the Serbs voted to remain within Yugoslavia, the plebiscite. One of the constituent peoples was ignored when this decision on the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina was made. This plebiscite is mentioned on several occasions, in documents, and it is considered to be a betrayal. All those who did not vote in the plebiscite thought that this idea of the Serbian People had quite simply been ignored, and naturally as a result they called them traitors because they hadn't shown any solidarity with the Serbian People as far as Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining in Yugoslavia was concerned. That's how we could interpret this. And naturally, they then requested that such people should also be deprived of their rights, the right to work. And again, this was not implemented at that time. At least, not in Banja Luka. It took quite a lot of time before this was made operational through subsequent decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They also demand that the same be done in the judiciary. Was that done? Was that demand implemented?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in the judiciary immediately either. That was done a little later because in the judiciary, there were still people who were not Serbs, and it was a little more difficult to implement this in Banja Luka because the population of Banja Luka was mixed. And in the parliament, there were various parties. And in a document, you'll see who there was from the Bosniaks and from the Croats, and there were even other nationalities that were represented. And of course, there were Serbs, too. It was a little more difficult to adopt such a decision. And finally, in the executive organs, well, my vice-president was a Bosniak, too. He was there until the end, until 1994 when he left. And at that time, the exodus of the Serb people from the Knin Krajina seemed inevitable with the agreement of Cornelio Sommaruga, they started leaving the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I do notice that the witness in all good faith and definitely meaning well is giving more information than he's being asked for. For the time being, I'm going to leave it in your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. hands to stop him when you feel it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you prefer that I will do that, then I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I can do that, Your Honour, if I feel it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And addressing myself to you, Mr. Radic, please try to answer the question, the whole question, and nothing but the question. There may be sometimes occasions when more information is good to have, but please try to restrict yourself to answering the question only, and don't give more information than you were asked for. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that Mr. Radic has some business engagements and would like to be able to leave here as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That would help him leave here as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If he would answer the questions just as briefly as possible, it will help him get out of here, I think, a little easier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I go to the next demand, Mr. Radic, and that is: "We are requesting from the supreme command and presidency of Yugoslavia not to break up the Banja Luka Corps and not even think about moving its assets to other places." Did this crisis staff that was created have any competency to issue orders to the supreme command or the presidency of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. The Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka couldn't do this, and not even the National Assembly of Republika Srpska could have done this. An order arrived from the main staff of the JNA requesting that all officers withdraw by the 15th of May and that they be transferred to Yugoslavia. Most of them obeyed this order and returned to Yugoslavia. But some of them remained there. I would like to tell you that that was the smallest corps in the JNA, and it consisted of about 1.500 men. I'm talking about the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The end part of paragraph 2 talks about officers in the Banja Luka Corps who had voted against Yugoslavia and who were in high positions handling valuable equipment which could easily be handed over to the enemy. And they request the transfer or replacement of those officers. Did this crisis staff that was created there in Banja Luka have any competence to transfer or replace officers in the Banja Luka Corps?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any competence, but I don't know based on what they reached the conclusion that many of those officers voted against Yugoslavia. These are assumptions which were supposed to provoke some other sort of reaction. But this is not something that they could have known. They couldn't have known that they voted against Bosnia-Herzegovina remaining in Yugoslavia, the plebiscite that I've already mentioned. It's more a matter of the materiel resources, the military resources being kept in that corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look now at the third demand, number 3. It is actually the 10th or 11th demand, but it's number 3 on the list. "We request the arrest of war profiteers and the publication of their activities and names." Was that demand implemented by this crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It wasn't implemented at the time. And the gentlemen who were involved in this still are not doing this. You still have profiteers who are benefitting in this way. Not even the names of those who were war profiteers were made public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Mr. Brdjanin felt about this demand, the arrest of war profiteers? Did you ever hear him express his views about it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: He expressed his opinion on many occasions, but this was never implemented for the simple reason that Brdjanin exercised a certain amount of authority, that he didn't have sufficient authority to implement this. On numerous occasions, on the television, on the radio, he discussed the problem of war profiteers, but this problem was not solved, and it still hasn't been solved to this very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of demands was he making regarding war profiteers if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: He usually said that they should be sent to the front because their business was conducted through the Republika Srpska, the Army of Republika Srpska. It was possible for them to pay so as not to go to the front. He knew about this, so he said that the best way to get rid of them is to send them to the front. These people were young people in the flower of their youth. They were not old people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to number 4 now. "We request replacements in the banks, Jugobanka in Banja Luka, and the Privredna Banka, Banjalucka Banka in order to prevent a monetary shock." I have two questions about that. First of all, do you know what they were talking about with regard to a "monetary shock"?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I know what a monetary shock is very well because I'm an economist. But here, it wasn't a matter of monetary shock. When Yugoslavia disintegrated, the currency that we used was the dinar. All the valueless money, all the valueless dinars came from Croatia through Livno and would arrive in Banja Luka and other towns. Bags of money would arrive there. And with those dinars, they would buy foreign currency from private businessmen, and they would also go to banks with this currency, with these valueless dinars which should have been burnt in the national bank in Belgrade as soon as Croatia decided to reject the dinar as a currency. They called this a monetary shock. In a certain sense it's true to call it a monetary shock if you buy foreign currency with worthless money. So the person who is selling the foreign currency is being impoverished. This happened in Jugobanka. The people who called themselves SOS men, they captured two Volkswagens in which there were plastic bags of such money, and there was also foreign currency in plastic bags. Foreign currency that had been bought on the market or taken out of Jugobanka because they had connections there. And German marks, dollars, Austrian shillings, would leave the treasury. This happened when Macedonia left, too. Valueless dinars arrived in that area via helicopters. By using helicopters. They called this monetary shock, and this is why they wanted to replace the director in Jugobanka, et cetera. And Banjalucka bank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these replacements done? When they requested these replacements in banks, did those replacements happen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary in Jugobanka, as soon as he heard what was at stake, he left Banja Luka. The director of Jugobanka was from Sado [phoen]. This was a branch of the central office in Sarajevo. This director called me, phoned me and asked me at least to return the Volkswagen Golfs to him. And if possible, he asked me to release two men who had been in prison because they were involved in the black market, in the currency black market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you respond to those requests?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said he wanted you to release the vehicles and the people.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I returned the Volkswagen Golfs, but I couldn't release the two persons who had been arrested and against whom criminal proceedings had been instituted. I didn't represent the police or the judiciary, so I was not in a position to release the people who were involved in foreign currency -- in foreign currency black market.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are the Privredna Banka and the Banjalucka Banka two banks, two different banks?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, they're not. The Privredna bank was a branch of the Sarajevo Privredna bank. But before the war, perhaps one year before the war, the Privredna bank was separated, and the Banjalucka Banka Ltd. was established. It's one bank, but it has two names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the replacement requested made in that bank?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: A sort of selection was made. I think Mr. Began, who was the director, was replaced. And I think he was replaced by Mr. Poparic. I think that's what happened, but I can't say with certainty. I think this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was done, but I don't know. There was a sort of selection, and those who had access to the treasury and to foreign currency, this concerned them in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the purpose was to stop the monetary shock, the speculation in currencies and so forth. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. That is about as leading as you can get on a topic which Mr. Ackerman knows is an issue in this case, and that is why people were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I think I was summarising what he had already said. Just trying to summarise it. I think he already said that was the reason for these, because of the monetary shock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I think he said, his very first answer actually was in the sense that it wasn't really this. Let me take you back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I can just ask the question a different way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, you've made a statement. So let me just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with Mr. Ackerman. If Mr. Ackerman just changes the form of the question, that will be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of requesting these replacements? Do you know why they were requesting these replacements?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: In order to put an end to selling foreign currency for the valueless Yugoslavia dinar, which was no longer legal tender. The krona had already been introduced in Croatia. It wasn't legal tender in Macedonia either. So naturally whenever a certain currency is abolished in a country, it's handed over to the National Bank which burns this currency. So what should have been burned was used in order to buy foreign currency, and the Republika Srpska did not have much foreign currency. In any case, that was the purpose. But a monetary shock, that's quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So were these acts --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That tallies with what I was going to point out, referring to page 18, last three lines and the first ten lines of page 19 of the transcript. But he's now crystallised the position, so you don't need to go into further details. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if these actions that were being taken in these banks that the SOS is complaining about, just if you know, were these actions legal or were they illegal?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: You mean selling foreign currency?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Illegal. They were illegal acts because if an official enters the treasury and leaves with German marks after not having paid for them with dinars, naturally this was an illegal act. It could not have been a legal act. As far as JUG bank is concerned, it came to light that the person who was the director at the time was aware of such transactions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to number 5. "We request replacements in the post office where management positions are occupied by those who voted against Yugoslavia and who cannot, therefore, work in a united Yugoslavian PTT." Do you know if that demand was carried out?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I think that this demand was carried out, bearing in mind the nature of the post office service and bearing in mind the fact that the war was already raging after the Lisbon document, Cutilheiro document had been rejected. And people were afraid that the post office might be a focal point where information would be gathered. And I have to say that the first thing that was done in Croatia and in the federal part of Bosnia and Herzegovina was to dismiss people who weren't Croats or other Bosniaks from the post office, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me see if I can understand. You said, and maybe -- let me find it. You said you think it was carried out bearing in mind the nature of the post office. Can you expand on that? What was the nature of the post office that would cause this to make any sense at all?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, all contact established in Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia and Croatia, et cetera, all these contacts -- all such communication would be established by the post office. And naturally, it was easy to intercept conversations because there weren't very good protective measures against intercepting conversations. And when I first started performing my duties, my phone was tapped, and I informed the director that this was being done from a centre in the post office. I informed the director of this. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at number 6 now. "We request that the work of municipal organs be re-examined because it emerged that there have been abuses." Do you know what that is about?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't know, and I find it rather strange because the executive organs of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, I, as its president, I acquired them as late as June 1991. I didn't have any executive organs before that. And that is when I resigned, and I said I wouldn't continue working without any executive organs in place. That is why I'm finding it so strange to see that they might have done such huge abuses. They only had nine or ten months of work behind them if they were set up in June 1991, which is a fact, and the demand here was made on the 3rd of April 1992. So they had quite a short time to do so much abuse, and for them to be removed for their positions. That's why I'm saying that I did not accept any shake-ups in these organs, and people continued working long after that in the municipality. That is, those who were in their positions at the time when this request was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go now to the final demand here, number 7. "That extraordinary sessions of the Assembly of the municipality and of Krajina be scheduled at which the crisis staff would appoint its representatives to expedite these requests and at which the rights of soldiers, returnees from the front, and families of fallen soldiers would be adopted." Do you understand that demand at all, and was anything done in response to that demand?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That the SOS sends the message to the fighters to remain in the front, and for us, that is the SOS, we'll look after security of the town and of their dear ones, and that we will make sure that they will return to their own country as heroes. If there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't get any interpretation at all for the first part of his answer, and I'm not sure what's now being interpreted is whether the first part of his answer or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm actually trying to understand how to fit in what he is saying with the question. And perhaps let's start from the beginning and we try to make it understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think there was any interpretation at the beginning of the answer, which is why it doesn't make any sense at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I put too many questions at one time, Your Honour. So maybe I can break it down into a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can do that. And Mr. Radic, please take it as if you have not answered this question already, and you start from the beginning again. All right, this particular question only with regard to number 7.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't answer the question. I just wanted to establish a link between that question and the last paragraph. But let me first answer the question, and then I will point your attention to the last paragraph of the proclamation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me break the question up into a couple of questions, and maybe that will make it easier. The first part of number 7 seems to request Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that extraordinary sessions of the assembly - I assume that is the assembly of the municipality - and of the Krajina be scheduled at which the crisis staff would appoint its representatives to expedite these requests. Does that mean anything to you and was anything like that done?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is correct. They want extraordinary sessions of the Municipal Assembly to be scheduled. That's their first request. Can I now continue? May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. In the meantime, technicians, please note that we have lost everything on our monitor, except that Judge Taya has got the transcript back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mine just came back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So their request was for the extraordinary sessions to be scheduled for the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. At these sessions, the crisis staff would appoint their commissioners, as they called them, whose task would be to implement the aforementioned requests. At these sessions, also rights of fighters and their families would be adopted. This, indeed, was carried out. However, since they only had a minority in both of these assemblies, this was not implemented. And now, if you will allow me, I would like to tell you what the goal was of all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The goal was what is contained in the message, in the last paragraph. And the message was those who were on the front line, stay there, and the rest of us will take care of other things. We will make sure that we become an integral part of the government, both in the town and the ARK Krajina, instead of being on the front lines with these people. What they wanted to have was power. They didn't very much care about the implementation of the ideas in the proclamation, and that is the main point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like to know is why, instead of listening to these people in -- this crisis staff and all these things, why didn't you just have the army or the police arrest them or throw them out of town?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: If you look at the date when all this was happening, you will see that this was happening when the army was withdrawing from Slavonia. The army was regrouped and starting to look after the deblocking of Krajina which was cut off from the rest of the world. These forces were on their way back. They returned. They regrouped themselves. And as we like to say it, they broke the corridor towards Serbia. I would like also to remind you, and I'm sure you'll find it in a document somewhere, that at that time, 12 babies died in the clinical hospital centre. Those were prematurely born babies. And they died only because they couldn't receive the oxygen that was necessary to keep the incubators running. That was the reason why the corridor had to be opened. And that is when the groups were formed and when forces were grouped somewhere around Doboj and how could they look after the problems that started arising somewhere in Banja Luka, for example. And if you ask me why the police did not intervene, I suppose that they were also called to be on the strength of the army. And secondly, Mr. Ackerman, I, during the war, my predecessors before the war, and the mayors nowadays are not in the position to give any orders to the police because they have their chain of command. Whether they received any orders to that effect or not, I really am not in a position to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm finished asking you questions now about SOS, and I want to ask you now to look at Exhibit P168, please. You should have in front of you a document signed by Nikola Erceg dated 5 May 1992 which forms a war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Is that the document you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It lists several names there. If you look at number 5 on the list, it, I think, has your name. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to 5 May 1992, were you made aware in any way that you were going to be appointed as part of this war staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that you had been appointed to this group?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, I received this decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So somehow, this decision was sent to you or delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Not somehow. It was delivered by mail, and I received this as a decision issued by the autonomous region, or better say, the executive council of the autonomous region whose signatory was Mr. Nikola Erceg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then begin attending meetings of this war staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I must say that I don't remember. I attended meetings really very rarely, and I really didn't know what this war staff was supposed to do in the first place. You must bear in mind that this was already the time when the army was engaged in preparing for the breakthrough of the corridor. It was on the 5th of May, and these preparations were very far ahead. And I believe that war operations may have even started at the time. And this type of a war staff, even if they did do something, the only thing that they could do was things that had to do with logistics. They could provide for the necessary food, clothing, footwear, and fuel for the army vehicles. I must say that the war started and that the state was not nonexistent. And it was the municipalities that had to bear the brunt of the war operations in terms of the supplies for the army and in terms of supplying the families of those who were on the front lines. So if you have any documents or minutes, I would really be curious to see what was done by the war presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You raised something that I do want to follow up with you about. You talked about logistics, providing food, clothing, footwear, and fuel. Was that a task that was -- that was unusual? Was it specific to this particular time in 1992, or was that something that had been a municipal civilian responsibility in the past with regard to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The JNA was a well-established system, and it was well known who was in charge of supplying food, fuel, medicines, ammunition, weapons. All the formations which were on the strength of the JNA were supplied from the centralised institution. I don't know where that was, I was not a soldier. But I -- there was a centralised supplies system. And that's how all the units of the former JNA in Yugoslavia were supplied. Municipalities were under no obligation to provide supplies for the units of the JNA on their territories because a large portion of the budget of Yugoslavia was allocated for the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did that become a responsibility, then, of the municipalities in 1992? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I have just told you. A state was proclaimed, but this state did not have its budget. Or even if it had its budget, it was so meager that it could not provide for any financing of the war. And when all the youth left Banja Luka, and a lot of them left, and a lot of them were killed, then it was Banja Luka's obligation to provide these young men with clothing, footwear, food, medicines. And later on, it was also prescribed that the municipalities should also look after their families, their wives, their children, even their elderly parents. This is what we were tasked with by an enactment that we received. But that was much later than this 5th of May 1992, which was the early days of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back now to the ARK Crisis Staff that you were appointed to. How many meetings of that ARK Crisis Staff would you say that you attended? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I said few. Mr. Blagojevic, who was the secretary, says that I attended once or maybe twice. But I would like to see either documents or minutes that would show exactly how many times I attended. I did not attend the crisis staff meetings many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were aware that meetings were being held and that you were not attending. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: If I didn't go, then I would delegate my secretary to go there to see what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you go? Why didn't you attend all these meetings?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, Banja Luka is a big place, and I had other things to do. The first meeting that I attended showed me that this was not an institution that could be of any use to me when it came to my primary tasks. And that was the protection of the town and protection of its citizens. It would really be good if we could see documents and minutes of the meetings. This would show us what the -- what they were involved with, what they were set up to do and what they actually did during their work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what went on in however many meetings you attended -- the one or two or however many. Can you recall what went on in those meetings? What were they like?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know if there was ever a meeting held that would be attended by all the members of the AR Krajina Crisis Staff. There were always people missing. The contents or the agendas of these meetings that we had received were not the true reflection of what was really going on. So I concluded that attending those meetings would be a waste of time because nothing important went on there. I drew that conclusion based on the documents that I had received. Even if they reached a conclusion or a recommendation, then they would have to be ratified by the Municipal Assembly. We would analyse the legality of such conclusions, and then we would also analyse the possibility of their implementation. All in all, this was basically the reason why I decided not to attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just as a general proposition from your perspective, observing the work of that crisis staff, what role did that ARK Crisis Staff play in the events in the Krajina between the 5th of May and the 17th of July 1992, if any?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war broke out, there was an association of municipalities. Then the AR Krajina was established. The goal was to exchange information on possible problems and help each other. That was the original goal. The Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina is not something that just turned up. It was not something that was created in Banja Luka by an individual. There is a document which reached us signed by the prime minister, and according to this document, the crisis staff was to be set up with certain obligations. However, this crisis staff did not carry out the tasks that had been set out by that document. Let me even be so bold to claim that this was just a transfer of authorities. But this body was not empowered in keeping with those authorities. Those people who serviced the crisis staff did not have the resources to pay their salaries, for example. And although they may have been perceived as the highest organ of government, however, they were not in the position to influence any changes if they didn't have any material resources. So what kind of a power is that? What kind of a government is that? The municipalities which joined the AR Krajina which had representatives in the crisis staff, especially the poorest municipalities amongst them, stopped attending those meetings. And that is the only thing that I remember about the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crisis staff in relation to the army, did Mr. Brdjanin or the crisis staff itself exercise any control of any kind over the army?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Nobody but the presidency or the first figure of the presidency could exert any influence over the army or the police. Nobody had that power. I would like to remind this Honourable Chamber that not before the war, not during the war, not even today civilian organs have had any influence on the army. Not even today when there is a mayor of Banja Luka, that person cannot issue any orders to the police. All he can do is to issue a request, which is then forwarded to the Ministry of the Interior, and then it's the Ministry of the Interior which issued an implementation order. This question has already been put to me, whether Brdjanin was in the position to issue orders to the police or to the army. And I answered then and I'm answering now that no, he was never in that position. He was never in the position to issue any order to any military unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your answer also includes the police. I think you've included both the police and the military in your answer, that neither Brdjanin or the ARK Crisis Staff had any control or position to order. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I was already asked that, and I answered that he was not in the position to do that. He didn't have any competencies of that kind. Nobody would have obeyed any such order coming from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you were already asked that, I think you're referring to your conversations with the Prosecutor in Banja Luka. And it might help you if you understand that the Judges do not have those documents, so they don't know what you've already been asked. Okay?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That is not my problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think we can take a break now, Your Honour, if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before, and while Mr. Radic hears this, first of all, I don't know -- Mr. Ackerman mentioned that Radic had business appointments. I don't know how long Mr. Radic's thinks -- or Mr. Ackerman has told him he's going to be here. And that's the first question. But if he does have business appointments for this week, it may be as well to cancel them. Secondly, Your Honour, he said he brought with him a copy of Glas. I'm asking at this stage, otherwise I can wait till cross-examination, but I'm going to be asking for copies of any documents that he's brought with him. And therefore, I wonder if he would be prepared to hand them over now. In addition, I'm particularly interested in documents relating to the meetings of the municipal crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Am I being asked a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you have any comment. Otherwise I will direct the question to Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't have any comments about what Ms. Korner just said other than I think Mr. Radic understands that he is here until we're finished asking him questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long is your direct going to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will be finished today, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By and I -- if I've read you well it means that you will be engaging him in cross-examination until the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not-- I didn't realise-- I rather assumed that Mr. Ackerman had a lot more to get through than he obviously does judging by his list of the documents that he's given us. If he's going to finish today, no, then the answer is I probably won't take the rest of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's number 1. Number 2. Mr. Radic, did you bring with you any documents apart from the Glas newspaper that you mentioned earlier on in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it seems to me that everybody has access to this article. I've had it in my hands several times. It's the same article that I have just been shown here. So I have nothing new to give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that the only document that you brought with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have a break. In the meantime, I was going to suggest the following timetable for the -- for today. Is it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. your wish that we revert to the practice we had before, finish 6.30 instead of 7.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, I'm in Your Honour's hands on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is the case, we'll have a break now, and we will resume at 4.05. Is that agreeable with everyone? And we will then go for an hour and a half, until 5.35. And then we'll have another short break of 20 minutes, and finish at 6.30. We start at 5.55 and we finish at 6.30. Is that okay with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, I mean, it does seem we're only sitting for effectively half an hour after the second break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We could sit straight from 4.00 -- no, we would still need a break. What we could do is to shorten the break. But, I depend --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the interpreters, I think, Your Honour, that need -- I think it's got to be at least 20 minutes for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that for the time being. We start at 4.05, and then we break at 5.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, before we broke, you mentioned something about the minutes of the ARK Crisis Staff. If you have any idea where to find any of the minutes of the ARK Crisis Staff, we'd sure appreciate you sending them to us, because we have been looking for them, all of us, for months. Do you know where there are any minutes of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: You can find them with SFOR, SFOR, who took them away from the archives where they had been kept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, they were in the archives of the municipal building when SFOR came and took the archives away?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: They probably them took away from the archives. If they were there, they took everything that they were interested in. So it would be good to ask them where are those documents, whether they have those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: Was there ever a time during time of the ARK Crisis Staff when you as president of the Banja Luka Assembly wanted to do something and had to get the approval of Mr. Brdjanin or the ARK Crisis Staff to do it? Was there ever a time when that happened?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I can't remember there ever being such situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Brdjanin ever issue any orders to you, as the president of the Municipality of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I don't remember any such situations either. Perhaps they said something to that effect, but it really wasn't important, so I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he had ever issued any kind of orders to you from his post as president of the crisis staff, would you have been legally bound -- duty-bound to carry out those orders?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That would have depended on the order, whether it was an order that was legitimate or not. If it was an illegal order, I most certainly would not have implemented it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a mechanism did the ARK Crisis Staff have to enforce any of its decisions or conclusions? How could they enforce the decisions or conclusions that were issued by them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. As I said, they had received some sort of de jure authority. But as to whether they had authority to force someone to implement something like that, I'm not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people were employed, staff persons, by the Municipality of Banja Luka during the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: There were about 350, perhaps 380 staff members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know how many staff people were employed by the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Perhaps two. Boro Blagojevic was the secretary as far as I know, and perhaps there was another secretary who would take messages, et cetera. But as to whether there were any other members in that crisis staff, I don't think so. And I think that they're all volunteers in any case because I don't know how they could have paid these people since there were no funds with which to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the ARK Crisis Staff have offices, vehicles, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The crisis staff or the ARK?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the crisis staff was located in the building -- in the PIK Kozara building which is where the ministry for public utilities was located, and for urban planning. Its sessions were held in the municipality building on occasion, and sometimes when they didn't need that much space, they would hold sessions in the GIK Kozara [Realtime translation read in error "Gika"], across the road from the assembly, which is where Mr. Brdjanin worked before the war. But as far as vehicles are concerned, I'm not aware of him having had a special vehicle. If he did, it was provided to him, but he would usually use his own vehicle. But I am not aware of him having a lot of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at another document now. A bit of a change of pace. I'd like you to look at P1237, please. And I think you've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: There's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see here, it says 18, 16. It says Pika, P-I-K-A, instead of GIK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's line 38 -- page 38, line 18. It should be GIKA [sic]. Right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: GIK, yes. Not PIK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have the distinction of being the first witness in months of trial to correct the transcript for us.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It's professional deformation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have the English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because we've got 1237, not the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It should be 1237, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1327 is what you said, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is the number of that? Yes, but the document you have on the ELMO, 1237. It is 1237, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the right one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you're familiar with this document, are you not, Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything -- you know, from your position in government, is there anything about this document that strikes you as unusual in any way?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: As far as this document is concerned, I don't think I was aware of it until I was shown the document. It was drafted in Prijedor in the public security station. And it's signed by Simo Drljaca. And it doesn't say it's a decision of the crisis staff of the ARK here. Because there is also a Prijedor Crisis Staff. Everything that is stated here was dictated by Mr. Drljaca in the Security Services Centre in Prijedor. And as you can see, it was forwarded to the crisis staff. It doesn't say "Prijedor," but it was forwarded to the Prijedor Crisis Staff, to coordinators of the Security Services Centre, Jesic, Majstorovic, these aren't people from Banja Luka. And it was provided to the security Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. centre, to the chief of police, to the leaders, to those in charge of security, to the director of the mine Ljubija, and it was forwarded to the archives, too. I was not aware of this document because it concerned an entirely different town, and it was forwarded to different people. It doesn't say that it has to do with the decision of the Krajina AR. If it had been provided to the Crisis Staff of the ARK, it would have probably mentioned the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was going to be my question. If you look at the distribution list, you don't see the Autonomous Region of Krajina or the ARK Crisis Staff as part of the distribution, do you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at -- look at paragraph 15 and 16, please. What is your impression of the meaning of those two paragraphs? How do you interpret them?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Allow me to read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't like to interrupt too often, but why does Mr. Radic's interpretation differ from anybody else's interpretation who can read it? He says he's never seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He said he had seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I understand it, it was shown by you. He said he hadn't seen it before it was shown to him. I assumed it was by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, I don't see why I should stop the witness from answering the question. Mr. Radic, when you are ready.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously this concerns prohibiting anyone from informing people of the text, of the contents of this order, signed by Simo Drljaca who energetically asks that all personnel and authorised officials strictly observe these instructions. I haven't read through all of the instructions and I can't remember this, but that's what it is about. Everything is strictly prohibited. It's strictly prohibited to provide information to anyone about this collection centre. This document is dated the 1st of May. The collection centre could function without anyone being informed about it because this was strictly prohibited. That's how I interpret this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the date is actually 31st of May, I think, if you look. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No. At the top, it says -- yes, I apologise. You don't see the number 3. It says the 1st of May. So yes, it's May 1992. 31st of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know if Simo Drljaca was a person who had sufficient authority that people would pay attention to things like that he wrote in those two paragraphs? Were those things that would have been obeyed, or did he have no authority or power?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: This person is not alive now. But I would say that he had a lot of authority in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to a completely different subject --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: And he most certainly would have been obeyed by the people he forwarded this to, the chief of police, security personnel, et cetera. They had to obey him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go to a completely different subject now. I want to ask you about a person by the name of Jovan Cizmovic. Do you know of Jovan Cizmovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at the document DB306, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is also already exhibited. I mean, there are mistakes, but to re-exhibit already exhibited documents... This is P23262. I mean what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, can you check that, Mr. Ackerman. And if you agree, then we can refer to the already exhibited document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know if it's in its full form. This comes up a lot, Your Honour, and I'm going to explain this so you'll understand what's going on. I'm not deliberately making Defence exhibits out of what I know are Prosecution exhibits. The problem is that we have an electronic system, and we have gone through rather traumatic staff changes in the course of this trial, and some things have just not gotten done the right way because we keep having to change the people that are doing them. So if our system doesn't show that it's an exhibit in the case, then we think it's not an exhibit in the case. And that's why this happens. And I'm sorry that it happens, and I wish there was a way for me to solve it. But I can't solve it without having someone who is willing to put in a couple of weeks checking all of our records. And I don't have anybody that can expend that kind of time. The Prosecution has a surplus of people. Maybe they would loan us somebody to do that. That would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Only too happy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The part of this document I want to draw your attention to is right at the very end. It's the last decision in this Official Gazette of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 21 December 1991. Do you see the decision I'm talking about? It involves an appointment of Mr. Cizmovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: On the appointment of the coordinator of the governors and executive bodies of the Serbian Autonomous District and the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Jovan Cizmovic is hereby appointed coordinator of the Executive bodies of Serbian Autonomous Districts and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. The present decisions shall enter into force on the day of its adoption and the date of the adoption's decision was the 21st of December 1991. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of role he would have played in that coordinator position with regard to the executive bodies of the Autonomous Region of Krajina? Do you know anything about the role he played?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: You know, it's difficult to see that on the basis of this document alone. I wasn't a deputy. That decision was signed by Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik. It doesn't say what his competence is. I can only draw analogy to come to a conclusion because I was also appointed as coordinator, as a representative of the Municipal Assembly. Someone from Trebinje was to control me and to inform me of what I was doing in Banja Luka. Naturally, he was supposed to give me suggestions because someone might have thought that I should have proceeded in a different manner. So it is probably that this coordinator, but this occurred at a higher level, it is probable that he had the same role and had to control matters and inform the person who had appointed him of matters, and he -- his role would be to influence the work of the executive bodies of the Serbian autonomous districts and the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I assume that that could have been his role. The person who appointed him would have to receive information from him and also to provide him with information as to what he should do in Krajina in order to carry through some of their conceptions. This is what I assume. But one should ask the person who signed this decision because it doesn't state what the duties of this person were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
