utterances.text: Well, he won't talk to me. You said -- the transcript indicates that you said that you were appointed as coordinator. And I think what you really said, that a coordinator was appointed to sort of watch over you. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I couldn't be my own coordinator. They sent me a coordinator from Trebinje, a certain gentleman who appeared and spent a week with me. And at the end, he apologised and said that he couldn't work in the way that I worked. He left, and he thanked the person who sent him there from Trebinje. He went to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document that you have been referred to appointing Jovan Cizmovic says that he's appointed coordinator of the executive body of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ARK, for instance. Now, the executive body would be that executive committee headed by Nikola Erceg. Is that what that's referring to, or not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. The legislative body was the ARK Assembly, and the executive body, that was the president of -- the president of the ARK executive body was Mr. Nikola Erceg. There must have been something they didn't like, so they sent a controller, coordinator in to control things. I haven't had the opportunity of seeing this Official Gazette, but I have seen an Official Gazette in which they appointed a coordinator for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want to ask you a little bit about Banja Luka during 1992. What was life like in Banja Luka during 1992? Was it a dangerous place to be?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka was sealed off, cut off from the world at the period that we are constantly discussing. From April to June, Banja Luka was completely cut off from the rest of the world, and I would like to point out that at the time we had that tragedy of the children I have already mentioned, with the babies I have mentioned. I turned to the UN commission to ask them to allow me to bring in oxygen. They referred me to Alija Izetbegovic and Franjo Tudjman and said they should provide me with this. But they were the ones who were preventing this from being supplied. This was an area which was completely encircled by the forces that were opposing us. So I don't know what you mean when you say "dangerous." Perhaps life was difficult because food, fuel, and medicine wasn't being supplied, and there wasn't any oxygen to save those children with. So could you please explain in what sense you mean "dangerous".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Would it be accurate to describe Banja Luka during 1992 as a ghetto for non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: We were all living in a ghetto at that time. It's enough to say that we were encircled from all sides, and why should one say that only non-Serbs were living in a ghetto? The question was what were the checkpoints? Why were they set up in the direction of Jajce and Derventa? The Croatian and Bosniak forces were there, or towards Vlasic. We were surrounded by enemy forces until a corridor was opened up. We didn't have an exit towards Serbia then until that time. So why should you say that some people felt that they were living in a ghetto and that we weren't living in such a ghetto?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at another document now. This is P259. Mr. Radic, the only part of this document I'm really interested in having you look at is the very first page. This document is abridged minutes of a session of the Municipality of Banja Luka of 23 June 1992. This is seven weeks or so after the ARK crisis staff is formed, 24 days before it ends. And what I'm interested in are the 87 assembly members that attended that session. You see a list here of people who did not attend. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I can't see the list. I can only see the names of those who attended, 87 -- no, no. Yes, I can see that. But I can't see the list of those 87 who attended. Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only list this provides is the ones who did not attend. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just glancing at that list, there are persons who are members of the SDA, persons who are members of the HDZ among that list. Also, some SDS people. But do you know why the people from the SDA and the HDZ were not in attendance on 23 June at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when it was that the SDA adopted a decision on nonattendance. As for the HDZ, they never adopted a nonattendance decision, and they stayed our members until the very end, that is, members of the assembly. However, when I look at this list, and I have to remind you of the date when this happened, for reasons unbeknown to me, a number of SDS members are missing. A number of members of the socialist -- those were reformists actually. Again, those were Serbs, and they, however, did not attend. I don't know why. And also, there are -- none of those who seceded communists. I really can't tell you why they did not attend. But those from the SDA to remain until the end, Emir Basatlic -- and I can't remember the second name, these two in the assembly on behalf of the SDA remained until the very end, and the HDZ attended the sessions of the assembly all this time. I can't tell you why these people were not present at this particular session, but I would say that there are more SDS members and Serbs who belonged to other parties who were missing. Why they were missing, I don't know. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I must also say that some of these people on the list of Serb ethnic background were on the front line. I can see here the name of one those who were killed, Bogdan Maric. They were at the time on the front line, so obviously they could not for that reason attend a session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go to a completely different subject now. I want to ask you some questions now about a visit that you made along with some other people to the Prijedor Municipality in July of 1992. Do you recall going to Prijedor in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember who accompanied you on that trip? Who went with you to Prijedor at that time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: There was nobody. It was a joint visit by the people who were mentioned in the Kozarski Vjesnik. I can't give you all their names. I know there was Mr. Brdjanin, there was Mr. Vukic, there was myself. I really can't tell you who else was with me. But you can read it in Kozarski Vjesnik. I agree that the names of those that are mentioned in Kozarski Vjesnik were really with me in that joint visit to Prijedor. It was upon the invitation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to have you look at P1496 [Realtime translation read in error "P496"]. That will help you. Now you were just trying to tell us it was on the invitation. Do you want to finish that answer?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I am saying is that the invitation came from the people from Prijedor, the president of the Municipal Assembly, and all those who were members of the Prijedor government. And we responded to that invitation and went there. I believe that invitation was sent to Mr. Brdjanin, who then invited all of us to go there together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you should have an article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated 17 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, this is 29 May 1992, so I suppose that is not that. It's a part of a diary, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the wrong document. P1496. Is that 1496?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P284 is the article.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did we get the right one this time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Krajina representatives in Prijedor. I don't know what the document is. You have to tell me. Don't you? Let me just see here. As far as I can see, there's no date. What kind of a mark is this? This is 00319239. Is that the document that we were referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, something's wrong here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should be -- 319212 is the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here at the top I can see 319 -- yes, now I can see it at the top and some names are mentioned. Yes. Krajina representatives were Radoslav Brdjanin, Radoslav Vukic, Stojan Zupljanin, Predrag Radic, they met with members of the crisis staff and representatives of the public security station and so on and so forth. Yes, that is that. This is what you asked me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Kozarski Vjesnik, are you aware of whether that was a daily newspaper, a weekly newspaper, or what it was? Do you know anything about this newspaper?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It is a local newspaper, a Prijedor newspaper. I don't know whether it is a daily or a weekly. Judging by this here, it doesn't say what the publication day is. If it was on the 17 of July, and if it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. then published on Wednesday. It is possible that it was a daily or maybe a weekly. In any case, it is a local newspaper which very few people may have received in Banja Luka. But in any case, it says here that this is a war issue of Kozarski Vjesnik. I don't know whether this newspaper is still published in Prijedor at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it circulated outside Prijedor, to your knowledge? Was it available in locations in the Krajina, or was it just a Prijedor paper?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I never saw it in Banja Luka, whether it was circulated elsewhere, in some smaller towns. It is possible. Maybe in Kozarska Dubica, which is also -- or possibly in Gradiska. I don't know. I didn't look for it Banja Luka, so I can't tell you for a fact whether it was circulated in Banja Luka or not, or anywhere else. In any case, this paper dealt with the problems of Prijedor. Yes, sessions of the municipal SDS board, the regional boards, problems with people moving out of -- from Prijedor Municipality. So this newspaper dealt predominantly with problems in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In connection with this visit to Prijedor on that day, did you have occasion to visit a place called Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. My impression was that this was the reason why we were invited to go there. There was an initiative which came from the Prijedor authorities to move these detainees to a prison in Banja Luka, or maybe even to Stari Gradiska, which is across the River Sava. Obviously, this was not feasible because the capacity of the prison in Banja Luka was too small, and Stara Gradiska was rejected by the army. It was very risky to send people there because this was the area where there were still war operations being underway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at a photograph. I don't know the exhibit number, but I'll hand the photograph I have to the usher and it can be put on the ELMO, and maybe the Prosecutor can help me with the exhibit number at some point. Do you recognise what's in that photograph? It's easier for you to see if you look over on the ELMO probably.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I was there only once, in Omarska, that is, on that one occasion. And it seems to me that this here is the administrative building and -- thank you very much. So this is the administrative building, and this is the so-called separation. I don't know what they actually called this particular building. I'm not sure because the photo is rather blurred. I did not have the opportunity to see these two buildings on the left. I don't know which road we took to get there, whether we came from behind or whether we took this road in front of the building. But I believe that we took this road in front of the building. It's very difficult for me to say for a fact that I recognise this building in such a blurred photo. And I was there only once. But I should think that this is what I visited on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember where you parked when you got there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: We parked on the flank of that building, on the side of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point to the flank that you're referring to. You have to point over on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I believe that the entrance was here. Somewhere here. And that we stopped here on the flank of the administrative building. Somewhere on its side, on its flank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you can return that photograph to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's 1128.17, the exhibit number, for the purposes of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the 1128.17 that you have any clearer?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for the record, what you referred to as the place you parked was just to the right of the large red building shown in the centre of the photograph. Just as a general proposition, what did you see when you arrived there at Omarska that drew your attention? What did you see there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I saw people who were standing there. And something that irritated me, and I told them that, was the fact that they had three fingers raised up in the air and that they were singing the song "who is saying, who is lying that Serbia is a small land." When we entered the administrative building or the headquarters, I told them that this was humiliation of these people. I was very cross because this was something that should not have been done to the detainees. It was a form of mistreatment or mental abuse of these people. They were Bosniaks. And they should not have been asked to sing those songs. They told me that they did it with pleasure. I doubted it sincerely. I doubted they did it with a lot of pleasure. We didn't stay there too long. And as I was leaving, I was very, very angry having seen what was being done to these people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those songs that might be called Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, these were not Chetnik songs. There are other songs that are considered Chetnik songs. This song was sung by the Serbian fighters in the First World War, the Serbian army sang that, which liberated Serbia from Austro-Hungarian, and then this is what they sang. Who's saying whose lying that Serbia is a small land. It is not small. It waged three wars. At that time, there were no Chetniks when that song was sung during the First World War. However, this song was sung by the Serbs, and this was not a song typical of the Bosniak people, and this was not the right thing to do, to make them sing this song.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You believed it was humiliating to make them sing it. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you make any observations about the condition of the people that you saw there? Did they seem to be healthy, unhealthy? Could you draw any conclusions about their condition?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It was very hot, and they were standing outdoors. Whether they were all there, whether some who were ill were kept indoors, I don't know. However, those that I saw did not look exhausted to me. However, what I'm saying is that I believe that there were more of them indoors, and the conditions in there were not very good. The people that I saw did not look exhausted to me. I did not get that impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think there were people there who might have been in worse shape who were kept indoors and you didn't see? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that there were people indoors whom we couldn't see. Only some of them were lined up in front of the building. The others were indoors, so I can't say what the conditions of those people who were kept indoors was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you made your feelings known, you said, to the people when you went inside, to the people that were there running the camp, about the humiliation that you saw. Did you -- while you were there that day, either inside or outside as you were leaving, did you react in any other way to what you had seen in there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: First I told them inside that this was not a way to treat prisoners of war. That was my first observation. And secondly, when I stepped outside, I looked at those people again. There was a stone in front of me. I kicked it very hard. And they realised that what they were doing to these people was not the right thing to do, that this is not what should have been done. I repeated that when we went to the building of the municipality, and they promised that they would do their utmost to move these people as soon as possible to a safer and more humane place than that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you kicked a stone. What -- I mean, why did you kick a stone? Was that an expression of some kind?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: How else could I express my feelings? When you kick a stone, when you kick something with your foot, you know what expression -- what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. feeling you may be expressing. It was rage. I could have maybe done something else, but I chose to kick that stone. And members of my delegation noticed that, and they realised that something was amiss. They did not expect such a strong reaction on my part, and especially they did not expect me to tell them what I told them when we went to the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brdjanin see your reaction to what you'd seen there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I suppose so. Because he later told me that he had noticed this and that he also could see that I was very angry. I don't know whether he will also remember having said that to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he disagree with your anger? Or did he agree with it? Or did he do anything?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he kick any rocks?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I didn't see it. He may have. He may have reacted in that way, but I didn't see it. I only know that when we returned to Banja Luka, he did say that he had noticed me having been very angry and reacting in the way I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he say that in a way to make you believe he thought you were wrong or right or what? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The mere fact that he mentioned it, that he told me that means that he agreed with me and that he also agreed that the way those people were treated was not right. That is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Independent of that, do you have any knowledge about Mr. Brdjanin's feelings with regard to non-Serb people? Did he -- in his actions, things he did, did you see anything that would let you know how he felt about non-Serb people?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, you have to draw a line between the Brdjanin who appeared on TV and the Brdjanin in private life. On TV, he appeared as if competing with other individuals to see which one of them would say more things addressed to other people. That is his TV persona. In private life, he did things that only have been surfacing recently. The other day, Mrs. Halima Miskin from Mostar contacted me. She is a Bosniak lady. She told me that if need may be, she would come and testify before this Honourable Chamber as to how he had helped her. Those are the things that he did. And if you ask me why he didn't make it public, I have just one plausible explanation, and that is he did not dare. He did not dare make it public that he did good deeds by Bosniaks, by Croats, because it would have cost him his ministerial position and all the other things. And maybe some other unpleasant things would have happened to him. This is my impression about Mr. Brdjanin. At that time, when this was happening, I didn't have a clue that he was doing good things. This lady, Halima, contacted me of her own will. They were expelled from Mostar. They came to our Mesa [as interpreted]. Brdjanin helped them, found them accommodation, and she told me, therefore, if they want me to testify, I will testify on his behalf. This is what I can tell you about Mr. Brdjanin. There is written word. There are video and other footages, and Mr. Brdjanin cannot deny any of these things. But also there are witnesses who are ready to confirm that not everything about him was as black as it is being portrayed. I don't know whether it is okay for me to say this, Madam Prosecutor. I said to representatives of the OTP, and this was recorded, that this person never killed anybody. He never raped anybody. He did not participate in the creation of concentration camps or whatever you may want to call those places. But he did talk a lot, and I can vouch for that. He talked quite a lot. That is my opinion of Mr. Brdjanin. But he never killed anybody, he never raped anybody. He never incarcerated anybody himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this visit to Omarska, you went back to Banja Luka. Did you do anything about what you'd seen at Omarska when you got back to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The representative of the international Red Cross committee was Mr. Beat Schweitzer. I had very good cooperation with him throughout the war what he was in that position. I invited him and I asked him to meet me, and I asked him to do whatever is in his power firstly to record these people, and secondly, to find a solution for them, for them to be moved from that particular place. And he did that. It took a while. That is a fact. However, he negotiated with the army, and he secured a place for these people because the army was the only organisation that had such huge places, barracks. But all the troops were on the front line. People were then recorded, and then they were shipped by planes to various destinations all over Europe where they still reside. Many of them are not returning because they don't have anywhere to go back to. They don't have jobs to go back to. And the same applies to the Serbs. There are Serbs in Croatia who also don't have jobs. They don't have anywhere to live. And that's why they're not returning. And the Serbs in Croatia, who emigrated to Croatia, they also go back to Europe if they can because there's no livelihood for them here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was it after you got back to Banja Luka from Omarska before you got in touch with Mr. Schweitzer? Was it the same day, next day, when, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, you can't call him now. He was engaged. It was a matter of a day or two. And after that, I met him and spoke to him, and he reacted very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you ask Mr. Brdjanin to simply order that Omarska be closed and instruct the Prijedor authorities to close the Omarska structure? Why didn't you ask Mr. Brdjanin to do that? Could he have done that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: First of all, why didn't I make such a request. It's understandable. I was president of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka, and the authorities were there in Prijedor. But as to why Mr. Brdjanin didn't do that, the idea of suggesting this to him didn't even occur to me because he didn't adopt the decision that you showed me a minute ago here. This was a decision adopted by Simo Drljaca, so no one asked him about this affair. There was the Prijedor Crisis Staff, and it was forwarded -- from there, it was forwarded to the CSB, the Security Services Centre, and you will never find that it was forwarded to the crisis staff and to Radoslav Brdjanin personally. And if I had even mentioned this to him, he wouldn't have been able to do anything because he had no such authority because if he had had such authority he could have told them not to detain these people there. So the idea of suggesting this to him didn't even occur to me. I don't know whether this idea occurred to Mr. Brdjanin. You should ask him about that. But if he didn't make such a request, the only reasonable explanation I could provide is he had no such authority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did Mr. Brdjanin have authority over the people in Prijedor? Could he order those people to do things and not do things? Did he have that kind of authority?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at DB - this is another subject now - DB286, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO? We don't seem to have it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Somewhere. It should have been in the batch of documents that was delivered today, but it has been an exhibit before. I just couldn't find the number. But here it is. Here's an English one you can put on the ELMO. Unfortunately, I've got some marks on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that I've shown you before, Mr. Radic. It's dated 23 August 1992. It's a document authored by Colonel Vukelic, and it regards an attempted visit to Manjaca by Tadeusz Mazowietski. Now I know you have a long version of the story about this document. I'm really more interested in the short version. It's the case, isn't it, that Mr. Mazowietski didn't actually get inside Manjaca on that day that he came there?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your role with regard to this visit by Mr. Mazowietski? Why are you mentioned right there at the very beginning of the document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Because as it says in this document, the ministry of foreign affairs, Mr. Bula, and Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic the vice-president sent me a protocol for the visit of Mr. Tadeusz Mazowietski in which it said that when he entered the territory of Republika Srpska at the River Sava near Gradiska, it's stated who he should meet in Banja Luka, in addition to myself, who was to receive him. He was supposed to meet Bishop Komarica, his holiness from the Orthodox church. And he was supposed to visit Mufti Ibrahimovic, a Mufti representing the Islamic religious community. Mr. Mazowietski appeared. I merely tried to address the matter of the protocol and ask him whether he agreed with it. He refused to discuss the protocol that had been signed either by Koljevic or Buha. That he requested that he go to Manjaca immediately. I told him that there was a protocol and that I couldn't authorise him to visit a military facility because I'm a civilian. I was a civilian, not a military person. He asked me what should be done. I said that the military authorities had to be consulted, or the military organs. I informed the staff command of the matter. They forwarded the affair to the General Staff, to the Main Staff, and then they attempted to reach an agreement. While trying to reach the agreement -- well, Mr. Mazowietski was finally authorised to go up there. He was received by the military organs, and the person who signed this, Mr. Milutin Vukelic, the colonel who drafted this report and sent it to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, in the end, they didn't let him in because it was -- the night was falling. People had been taken to their accommodation, and they didn't want to let him in. And there was this protocol, and this wasn't in accordance with the protocol. That's why I'm mentioned, because this was forwarded to me. I received this, and the gentlemen in the 1st Krajina Corps also received it. And they knew what the protocol had provided for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you look at the very last page of that document, there's a paragraph that begins: "Regardless of the consequences..." And right at the end of that, it says: "... Which can be confirmed by those representatives of the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina who were present and who spoke with him." Can you recall who was present and who spoke with Mazowietski from the Autonomous Region of Krajina on that day?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I'm pretty certain that Mr. Brdjanin wasn't present. But as to whether Mr. Erceg or someone else was present, I don't know. But he says that we can confirm this, but we didn't confirm this because I can't judge whether he came to visit for intelligence or humanitarian reasons. He as the security official could judge this. But because he didn't appear in the territory where I was the president of the Municipal Assembly, this was a military facility and a civilian can't enter such a facility without authorisation. His conclusions, his conclusions they are not mine, although as I say it's odd that a diplomat of his rank doesn't respect the protocol that he accepted and he signed and set off on this visit in accordance with the protocol. He didn't see the Mufti, he didn't see the Vladika, the priest from the Orthodox church. But he came to this bishop in a strange way and after a long time had passed, when he should have already left the territory of Republika Srpska. We should bear in mind that the war was raging at that time. It was on the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we're finished with that document. I want to change now to a new subject. I'd like you to look at P255, please. You should have in front of you a decision of the crisis staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina of 22 June 1992. And while we're looking at a document from the crisis staff, I'm wondering if you have had occasion to look at documents issued by this crisis staff and pay any attention to whether they were all signed by Mr. Brdjanin or not. Do you have any knowledge about that at all?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: As you can see here, this has been obscured, and especially the part where it says "the president." As far as I know, this isn't Brdjanin's signature. It's not his signature. I don't know how you interpret this. I don't know whether you think someone could interpret -- could sign this on his name. I don't know whether someone had this authority. But the document such as it is -- well, I don't know what you're interested in in this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not very interested in what I just asked you about, but I was interested whether you knew anything about it or not. What I do want to ask you about was the material that's contained there in I about posts not being held by employees of Serbian nationality who have not confirmed by plebiscite or who in their minds have not made it ideologically clear that the Serbian Democratic Party is the sole representative of the Serbian people. It sounds like what that decision is saying, that you have to be a member of the SDS to hold one of these more important positions. That seems to be what it's saying. Were you aware of this decision around the time that it was issued?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I was aware of it, but in the third paragraph where it says that those who did not vote in the plebiscite for Republika Srpska, those who were outvoted in the referendum, or it would be better to say were excluded from everything that was taking place. Well, I ask myself how someone with proof that he had not voted in the plebiscite since this was done in secret. But that the SDS is the only representative, this has another consequence because they also tried to replace directors of Serbian nationality who were not SDS members. I managed to find out about this, but these people who were directors but weren't SDS party members, they were most involved in logistical matters, in supplying the families of combatants in Banja Luka and in supplying clothes and footwear, and even the director of the footwear factory was involved in this. Thanks to Mr. Karadzic, I managed to prevent these people from being replaced. But as far as the rest is concerned, would you like to ask me the second part of your question? I've responded to the first part of your question and I told you what I thought about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said something that makes me very curious. You talk about people who were not -- people who were heads of institutions -- I can't remember your -- people who were directors who weren't SDS --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Companies --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Who were not SDS members, and you say: "Thanks to Karadzic, they were not replaced." Tell me about that. What's that mean?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That means that preparations had already been made for their replacement because they were not SDS party members. I always believed that it was important for a director to know how to do his job well. It wasn't important for him to be a member of this party or that party. So at a joint meeting, I informed -- I introduced these people to Karadzic. I informed him about these people, and he said that they should not be affected, although they were not party members, because these were directors of the footwear company, of the brewery, of Incel, et cetera, and these people were supposed to be replaced. But I have to say that this was not just Brdjanin's opinion [as interpreted]. I have said that the term -- the differentiation of personnel was a euphemism. They have come up with a pretty word for something that is ugly. The differentiation of personnel, and this doesn't apply only to Banja Luka; it applies to Republika Srpska as a whole. Rationalisation living quarters was also a euphemism, and that was a term that covered many things, moving people out of their flat. Such things occurred because socially owned flats were taken over by people, and combatants from those companies would end up on the front line, and these companies would exert pressure in order to find accommodation for their children. But these people have got their flats back. It was nothing new. This is something that happened in Sarajevo, too. And to this very day, there are still people in Sarajevo who haven't got their flats back. The situation is the same in Zagreb. You have Serbs who have not been able to return to their flats or houses. So nothing new happened as far as this so-called differentiation of personnel is concerned. Call it what you will. I have to say that recently I had a document in my hands in which I was criticised for not conducting such a differentiation, for not having replaced people in banks. I thought that the people who were employed in these banks were good at their jobs, and this is why they remained there, at least to the extent that this would have been in my power.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, the transcript, I think, has an error in it. Page 65, line 5, it says -- you were talking about all these efforts being made to replace these people that were not SDS. You say, "But I have to say that this was not just Brdjanin's..." The transcript says "opinion." But I'm told that what you said: "I have to say that this was not just Brdjanin's product." Which is correct, opinion or product?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That was his specialty [as interpreted]. That was the case throughout Republika Srpska. He had to receive an order to do this, and Banja Luka was always inspected, and they would always say there was something that we weren't doing what was done elsewhere. So this was not his specialty. This was a general a rule, not just in the Republika Srpska, but also in the federal part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in Croatia, and so on. People from the federal part would come to us from Croatia, and they would tell us how they had lost their jobs and their flats only because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've got it wrong again. On line 66, page 8, it says: "With regard to Brdjanin, you said this was his specialty", according to the transcript, said "this was his specialty." And I'm told that what you said was "this was not his specialty." You said "not," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It was not his specialty. He didn't have authority to adopt such decisions. He had to receive such decisions, and this was done throughout Republika Srpska, not just in the crisis staff where Brdjanin was the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you one more question before we take the next break. I want to ask you this - and I don't know; I'm just curious about this because it came up the other day - would it make any difference with regard to this document whether or not it was published in the Official Gazette? If it was never published in the Official Gazette, does that make a difference?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, when it says the decision was adopted on the -- entered into force on the day of its adoption -- when it says that it enters into force on the day of its adoption, and it will be published in the Official Gazette of the autonomous region, well, this is the rule. And that's why I said I find it very strange that the president's signature is not on this document. I don't know what the reason for this is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happens if it's not published? Does that make any difference as to its effect? If it just isn't published, does it make any difference? I know it says it's going to be. But assume it wasn't published. Does that make any difference?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Well, it does make a difference obviously. For example, the second paragraph here, I didn't allow it to be implemented. It depended and varied from municipality to municipality. In some cases, people could hardly wait to follow such instructions. But I had people who were not SDS members, and I did not allow them to dismiss people and have them replaced with someone else. But from the legal point of view, whether it's a difference because here it says that it enters into force on the date of its adoption, and it will be published in the Official Gazette, this isn't a good way to put it either. A good way to put it would be that eight days after its publication in the Official Gazette, it would enter into force. But if this is what it states, then it means that it can enter into force without being published in the Official Gazette, which is not right. What is the purpose of the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you didn't allow this to be implemented in Banja Luka. What kind of trouble did you get for not implementing it? Did you get in a lot of trouble?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I had -- I could have had problems. But as I said at that meeting, at that common meeting where the president of Republika Srpska was also present, and those from his core circle who participated in that, well, he quite clearly told him that that shouldn't be done. If he hadn't said so, perhaps I would have suffered the consequences. But again, as I said, this could have only been forwarded from a higher level than the one that I received instructions from. Why did the army come to Banja Luka to try to discipline us? There were no mass graves. There was no massive destruction, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. This would be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll take another break now of 25 -- 20 minutes. So we will reconvene at -- 20 minutes from now anyway. 5.53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Just to inform you, Judge Janu had to attend to something urgent of a personal nature that came up unexpectedly. So we are proceeding, Judge Taya and myself, in virtue of Rule 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So are you prepared to certify that it's not because I've bored her to death. Your Honour, can we go into private session for a moment and can I ask that the witness leave the room for just a moment. It's a matter I really want to discuss privately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, there's a matter that we will need to discuss not in your presence, so please, Madam usher is going to escort you out of the courtroom for a while, and then we'll continue afterwards. Yes. Do we need to stay in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, could you please reaccompany the witness. And I'm going to explain the witness that this had absolutely nothing to do with him so that he doesn't get carried away with the idea that something is happening. Mr. Radic, I am so sorry for the interruption and the fact that you had to leave the courtroom. We needed to discuss something has got absolutely nothing to do with you. It's something strictly procedural and not involving your testimony. So my apologies once more. And we can now proceed. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I need the witness to be shown Exhibit P80, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you'll finish in half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I won't finish today, Your Honour. Contrary to prior expectations, I'll probably be -- looks like maybe one session tomorrow to get finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, you've seen this before. It's the Statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. I want you to first look at Article 35. You said at one point in your testimony earlier today that a decision of the ARK Crisis Staff had to go and be approved by the individual municipalities before it could be implemented. Is that in effect what Article 35 says, that decisions, conclusions of the assembly are only binding once they have been approved by the assemblies of the municipalities? That's correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other -- and you also said that with regard to this June 22nd decision we have been looking at, that you didn't implement it in your municipality. And do you believe that -- that this Article 35 gives you the right to make the decision as to whether to implement a decision or conclusion or not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph says: "The decisions and conclusions of the Assembly shall become binding for the member municipalities once they have been approved by the assemblies of the municipalities." In other words, until it has been approved by the Banja Luka Assembly, that decision cannot be implemented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to look at Article 38, and I just want you to take a look at the procedure that the statute sets out for how it can be amended, the procedure by which the statute is amended. And once you've become familiar with that, then I want you to look at P258, and keep P280 [sic] with you because we'll be using it again.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes. An opinion has to be obtained, i.e., after a lapse of a certain period of time, the assembly shall consider the proposal for the amendment of the statute and will submit it to the assemblies of the municipalities in order to obtain their consent. Having obtained the consent referred in the preceding paragraph, the assembly shall declare the amendment to be adopted. I don't know what your question is. What are you asking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to become familiar with you. I want you to look at P258. She has got it there. She can show it to you. I want you to look at decision 42, it's down closer to the end of the document. Number 42 dated 15 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: 42. I'm having a problem here. I can't find it. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in your language, you look at the bottom of the page, bottom right-hand corner, you have a number 00389000. It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 389. All right. Decision on amending the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Article 1, Article 35, paragraph 2, on the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina; Article 35, paragraph 2 of the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, in brackets, the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, number 1/92 is hereby amended and shall read as follows: "The decision and the conclusions of the assembly are binding for the municipalities." And that is Article 1. Article 2: "This decision shall come into effect on the day of its passing, and it shall be published in the Official Gazette of the Autonomous Region." And that is it. That's the end of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, bearing in mind what Article 38 of the ARK Statute says, do you have an opinion as to whether this decision of the ARK Crisis Staff effectively amends the statute of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, or does it not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: If there was a previous consent of the municipalities, and if the assembly of the AR Krajina passes and adopts these amendments, then what it says here, the decision and the conclusions of the AR Krajina assembly are binding for the municipalities, and this decision shall come into effect on the day of its adoption and shall be published in the Official Gazette of the autonomous region. I don't know. I'm not a legal expert, and I can't see any changes here, Mr. Ackerman. I don't know what is the change, the difference here. If a previous consent from the municipality has indeed been obtained, then already here it should read that the decisions and the conclusions are binding for the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was no previous consent, then it would not have been properly amended. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: In that case, decisions and conclusions of the AR Krajina assembly shall not be binding for the municipalities. They cannot be binding for the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're looking at 15 June of 1992. Do you have any idea why, if municipalities are respecting the decisions of the ARK Crisis Staff, why the ARK Crisis Staff would feel it necessary to try to amend the statute? Does that make any sense at all?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to tell you. But I don't see this being contrary to Article 38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go back, then, to P80. I want you to look at that again.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: This now, P80.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statute is what I want you to look at.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Statute, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this time, I want you to look at Articles 10 and 11. And first of all, tell us what Article 10 provides.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Article 10: "Other municipalities may join the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Paragraph 2: "A municipality wishing to join shall submit a request to do so to the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Paragraph 3: "Before deciding, the Assembly of Autonomous Region of Krajina shall obtain the opinion of all member municipalities." Do you want to hear an opinion on this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I think you've answered my question. It says that "other municipalities can join ARK," right, and gives the conditions under which that can happen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: This was not my response. This is what it says in Article 10. This reminds me of another article of the association of municipalities that existed before the war. Not every municipality had to be a member of the association. Those who wished to join, they joined. If they wanted to join subsequently, they could do that. So with slight modification, this is the exact copy of a document which regulated the relationship within the association of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina because such an association used to exist before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at Article 11 now --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: 11 is the same. 11 is the same. Every municipality can leave the autonomous region, and such a municipality which wishes to leave the autonomous region shall inform the autonomous region and the assembly of the associated municipalities. And you can leave the autonomous region only upon the lapse of one calendar year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So bearing that in mind --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: And I need to read the end: "The request to the leave the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall be submitted no later than six months before the lapse of one calendar year. A municipality wishing to separate from the Autonomous Region of Krajina is required to fulfill its obligations towards the Autonomous Region of Krajina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me ask you this: Is this organisation being described here, is this an association or is it a government?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: A government is a government. It is an executive body, and an association is something else. This is the association of municipalities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. A government is an executive body of the assembly of this Krajina which was the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the association itself, with its executive committee and its -- at one point its crisis staff, the whole thing, does it have the characteristics of a government, a political entity that governs, or is it just a voluntary association of municipalities? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: It transpires from this that this is a voluntary association of municipalities. At the moment you have an option whether you can join or not. It is voluntary. So the moment you can separate from an association, then this association is a voluntary association of municipalities. It is not fixed. So it is the free will of any one municipality whether to -- they will join or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at DB292. And I'm still basically talking about the 22 June decision of the ARK Crisis Staff regarding the dismissal of personnel. Now, what you should have before you is a -- part of a newspaper article, page from a newspaper. And it talks about a session of the executive municipal board of the Banja Luka Municipality. I want to direct your attention to the second paragraph. And it reads as follows: "Anton Ruzic who reacted to the decision of the Crisis Staff of AR Krajina on realisation of personnel policy. By that policy, it has regulated among other matters that only those Serbs who proved their loyalty by taking part in the plebiscite and who think that SDS is the only representative of the Serb people can hold the most important functions in business companies and institutions, working on behalf when we will be held responsible for certain decisions in the economic and social life" - that's Ruzic - "and added that regional government can request certain decisions from municipal bodies but not that they could work instead of the municipal executive board." Now, who is Ruzic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Anton Ruzic was the vice-president of the executive board of the Banja Luka Municipality. He is a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, could I ask -- is this Glas? It's not clear from what we have been given.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm quite certain it is, Ms. Korner. I'm quite certain it's Glas of June 22nd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could verify that and let me know afterwards, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I believe the record I have indicates that it comes from Glas, Your Honour. I'm just certain that it's from Glas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, let's proceed. So I take it that Mr. Ruzic was a Croat by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on June 26th, 1992, Mr. Ruzic is still participating in the government as vice-president of the executive board. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he's criticising this personnel decision of the ARK Crisis Staff saying that his view is they can make requests of municipal bodies, but they can't control municipal bodies or work instead of them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the document reports the remarks of Rajko Kasagic who was the president of the executive council. It says he gave numerous examples from the previous war when Germans and Japanese were removed from the Australian and American state bodies, and he reminded that Slovenia was the first to start such an approach on the Yugoslav territories, and Croatia was following that example, "that it is no better in Bosnia-Herzegovina where Serbs simply observed how were the others doing it," said Kasagic. And then go down, he says: "Besides I am against that Crisis Staff takes over the power in Banja Luka more so, since the other smaller municipalities in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are not putting into effect its decisions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It appears that Mr. Kasagic is aware that the municipalities in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are not -- are basically ignoring the ARK crisis staff. Were you also aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic probably knew it, but even more important than that was that Banja Luka municipality itself did not implement this decision of the crisis staff. Otherwise, Mr. Ruzic would not have been vice-president or would Mr. Kusmic, a Bosniak, who is not mentioned here, would have been the secretary of the inspection services, not to mention a number of others who still worked in the Municipal Assembly. However, Mr. Kasagic says another thing here. He is not in favour of the crisis staff taking over in Banja Luka. The more so because these decisions are not implemented by other smaller municipalities. He doesn't mention the names of these municipalities. However, it seems that he was against the crisis staff interfering with the policies of the biggest municipality in the territory of Republika Srpska. That is obvious from this passage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you sit here today right now, can you think of any decision of the ARK Crisis Staff that was implemented by the Banja Luka Municipality, even one?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Could you please show me these decisions. A decision which was in keeping with the law would be implemented as a legal decision. What was not in keeping with the law, I must say that I disregarded it. I did not implement it. Sometimes I would even tear it apart, and I didn't suffer any consequences because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but my question is as you sit here right now --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: I can't remember any such decision. I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Staying on this subject of implementation of this 22 June decision, look at P272 again now. This is a document dated 1 July, I believe, of 1992. It also has the date 6 July on it. It's addressed to all of the SJBs by the head of the CSB, Mr. Stojan Zupljanin. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the remarks of Mr. Zupljanin after he has set out the decision, and take your time reading it if you want to, is he saying -- what is he saying there about whether the various SJBs were required to implement this decision or not? Is he saying that they have to implement it, or is he saying that they should not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: If you will just allow me to read it quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, take your time.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG RADIC
utterances.text: The interesting thing is what it says under paragraph 3. "People cannot be dismissed from work without the CSB being aware of that." This was done in some public security stations. Some other adequate solutions have to be sought for their removal to the tasks and jobs which are not contrary to paragraph 1 of this decision. In other words, this limits the execution of this decision which was adopted by the crisis staff, and he wants to have the control. Or maybe not him, but the public security station to control the employment, the dismissal, and the replacement of these people. This is nothing new under the sun. Let's have that clear. The public security station in Banja Luka was very autonomous in these dealings. And the only superior to this body was the minister of the interior in Pale. I as mayor did not have any authority. Mr. Brdjanin, as the president of the AR Crisis Staff, I don't know. But I as mayor could request them to do something. Whether they did it or not depended very much on the consent of the Ministry of the Interior. So this is nothing surprising when it came to the Security Services Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suppose this is the place we stop for the day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Radic, we are stopping here for today. We will continue tomorrow, and we'll finish with you by the end of the week. So we will -- Madam usher, you can escort the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have one matter I want to bring to your attention before we rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, Mr. Radic, you may leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had understood from the Prosecution that we should schedule this witness for the entire week, so that's what we did. And then I think it was Thursday of last week, Ms. Korner indicated that we might not take the entire week. So at that point, we made efforts to get another witness brought here. It was quite difficult, but we managed to accomplish it. That witness has been rescheduled and will arrive here on Thursday and will be prepared to testify on Friday. So I just wanted you to know that that's what we have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he Witness Number 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That would be Bojinovic. 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You confuse me. Okay. But you confused me a little bit. And you intend to finish with him on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I'm telling you why, because originally you had said two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've gone through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you've gone down to half a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've gone through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then it's two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've got to stop reading those numbers, Judge. It's just make you uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I am presiding, Mr. Ackerman, not you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Mr. Ackerman -- do you mean you will take one day in chief as opposed to -- because I thought you had given us a whole lot of documents, and if all those documents are going in through them, then he won't finish on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They will go in through him very rapidly, I think I really think -- we may not finish him on Friday, but at least he's here. If we have to carry on until Monday, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the next witness is not number 5, but number 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't have the numbers here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have them. We stand adjourned until tomorrow, 2.15, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tomorrow, isn't it, Your Honour that we're finishing early?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At 5.00. Or 5.30. If you want to start earlier, we can start earlier tomorrow if there is a room available. We will finish before 1.00 tomorrow in the other case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I've now found my numbers. Witness Number 5 we tried to bring, and she is one of those who is caught up in the we've run out of passports problem in Bosnia. They don't have any passports, so she can't come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a way. I am sitting in the morning in the Nikolic sentencing hearing. But I don't think we'll take up to 1.00 tomorrow. I think we'll finish early. So we could start, say, at quarter to 2.00, if there is a -- or half past 1.00. If we could start at half past 1.00. I am available, and I will just consult with Judge Janu who is not here and doesn't know what I am saying. But I am pretty sure that she will not have any objection. But you have to find a courtroom. We are sitting in Nikolic. We are sitting in Courtroom III in the morning, and we finish at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Courtroom 2 is available for the whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we can start at half past 1.00 here. If -- I don't want to force anyone. Don't misunderstood me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're entirely in Your Honours' hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, what I mean to say is if we can together cooperate to send this gentleman back home --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Ackerman is only going to take another hour and a half, then I'm pretty certain that I would conclude by Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we gain an hour or so tomorrow Ms. Korner, then that would ultimately mean that perhaps Witness Number 17 won't need to stay here the weekend. So, it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's not arriving until Thursday, so, as I understand from Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But if he's arriving Thursday --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can't put him on before Friday. It's not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. He will testify Friday. I see, I see. It's not going to make a difference. I thought we would gain a day. But we are not going to gain a day. So we'll remain the same. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of November, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
